items.prompt: Candidates are sorted, and a combination loop is choosing values at one recursion depth. Which rule skips value-equivalent sibling branches?

options.text: Skip candidates[i] when i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1].
Skip every value equal to any value already in the current path.
Skip the first occurrence and keep only later equal values.
Skip equal neighbors whenever i > 0, regardless of the current start.

feedback.reason: Sorted equal values should produce one sibling branch per value at the same depth.

blocks.text: Deduplicate siblings, not all depths

Because the input is sorted, equal values are adjacent. At one combination depth, indices start, start + 1, ... are sibling candidates for the same path prefix. The first occurrence of a value represents that value choice.

If i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1], the earlier equal value was already available as a sibling and produces the same value-level subtree, so the later sibling is skipped. In a child call start changes; i may then equal the new start, allowing another physical copy at a deeper result position.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Equal values may be legal at different depths when multiplicity permits. The first occurrence should represent the value choice at this depth. This can incorrectly remove a legal repeated value at a deeper level.

blocks.title: Scope rule
blocks.text: Use i > start to recognize a later equal sibling; do not turn it into a path-wide ban on equal values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_all_equal_globally: Equal values may be legal at different depths when multiplicity permits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_first_duplicate: The first occurrence should represent the value choice at this depth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_if_i_gt_zero: This can incorrectly remove a legal repeated value at a deeper level.

items.prompt: In unique-permutation generation with sorted values and a used array, when should a candidate equal to the previous value be skipped?

options.text: When the previous equal index is not used in the current path.
When the previous equal index is already used in the current path.
Whenever an equal value exists anywhere in the input.
Equal candidates never need special handling.

feedback.reason: If the previous equal occurrence is unused, choosing the later one would start a sibling branch equivalent to choosing the earlier one.

blocks.text: The earlier equal occurrence owns the sibling position
The standard sorted rule first rejects a used current index. For an unused index i, it also skips when i > 0, values[i] equals values[i - 1], and used[i - 1] is false.

If the earlier equal occurrence is unused, both occurrences are available at the same depth; choosing the later one merely swaps equal index identities and starts an equivalent value sequence. If the earlier one is already on the path, choosing the later occurrence consumes the input's second copy at a deeper position and is legal.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: That usage distinguishes an ordering within the current branch and should remain legal. This would prevent using multiple equal occurrences when the input multiplicity allows them. They can generate value-identical sibling permutations.

blocks.title: Permutation skip
blocks.text: Skip a later equal unused index only while its earlier equal representative is also unused.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.previous_equal_used: That usage distinguishes an ordering within the current branch and should remain legal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_equal: This would prevent using multiple equal occurrences when the input multiplicity allows them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.never_equal: Without a special sibling rule, distinct equal indices can start separate branches that generate the same value permutation.

items.prompt: Why is skipping equal values at every depth unsafe for combinations that may use two copies of the same value?

options.text: It can remove a legal branch that selects separate equal occurrences at different depths.
Equal values are never allowed in a combination.
Sorted input cannot be processed recursively.
Equal values always have the same index.

feedback.reason: Duplicate control should eliminate equivalent choice orderings without erasing permitted multiplicity.

blocks.text: Multiplicity belongs across depths
Suppose sorted input contains two indexed copies 1a and 1b and the result may contain [1, 1]. At the root, 1b can be skipped as a sibling equivalent to starting with 1a.

After choosing 1a, the child starts later and may choose 1b, producing the legal multiplicity. A rule that bans every equal value at every depth removes this child and changes the result set rather than merely removing a duplicate construction.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Multiplicity depends on the input and result contract. Sorting is compatible with recursive search. Distinct occurrences have distinct indices.

blocks.title: Multiplicity rule
blocks.text: Collapse value-equivalent siblings while preserving separate occurrences that the output contract may consume at later depths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_cannot_repeat: Multiplicity depends on the input and result contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_breaks_recursion: Sorting changes candidate order but remains fully compatible with recursive enumeration when the output contract permits that normalization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.indices_are_equal: Equal payloads can occupy distinct positions; 1a and 1b retain separate indices and together provide multiplicity two.

items.prompt: An input contains [1a, 1b, 2], where 1a and 1b have equal values but distinct indices. What distinction must the solver preserve before applying value-level deduplication?

options.text: The two occurrences are separate candidate positions even though their values are equal.
They are automatically the same candidate object.
Only one occurrence exists logically.
Sorting makes their indices identical.

feedback.reason: Candidate identity and result equivalence are different layers.

blocks.text: Occurrence identity precedes value equivalence
Index identity answers which physical occurrence is chosen. Value equivalence answers whether two completed value sequences should count as the same output. These are separate contracts.

For [1a, 1b, 2], used-index state must distinguish 1a from 1b so the solver can use each at most once and can use both when multiplicity permits. Duplicate control may still choose one canonical order for equal occurrences to avoid emitting value-identical permutations.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Equal values do not imply identical positions. The input explicitly contains two occurrences. Sorting reorders positions but does not merge occurrences.

blocks.title: Two-layer model
blocks.text: Track indices for legal resource use; apply value-level equivalence only to canonicalize outputs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_object: Value equality does not merge two indexed positions into one candidate object; each occurrence can be consumed separately.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_count_only: The input explicitly supplies two occurrences, so the solver must preserve multiplicity two before deduplicating equivalent value orders.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_identity: Sorting reorders positions but does not merge occurrences.

items.prompt: Why is generating every index permutation and deduplicating completed value sequences with a set usually inferior to preventing duplicate branches?

options.text: It explores many equivalent branches and pays to hash or compare completed outputs.
A set necessarily changes the values inside each permutation.
Result deduplication makes recursion impossible.
Proactive control always requires illegal sorting.

feedback.reason: Proactive duplicate control reduces the search tree before equivalent work is performed.

blocks.text: Post-hoc deduplication pays for duplicate work first

With equal values, several indexed permutations can map to one value sequence. Generating all of them still performs every recursive transition and copies each length-n path before the set can discover equality.

A proven proactive rule removes equivalent branches near their common parent, reducing descendants, path copies, hashing, and temporary allocations. A result set can still produce the correct final value set, but with the larger generation cost and additional stored keys.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A set can store sequences without modifying their elements. The method is possible but inefficient. Sorting is legal when input order is not part of the output contract.

blocks.title: Cost boundary
blocks.text: Deduplicating after emission removes repeated outputs, not the search and copying work that created them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.set_changes_values: A set can store sequences without modifying their elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_impossible: Recursive generation still works; the defect is avoidable duplicate exploration and output-processing cost, not impossibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_not_allowed: Sorting is legal when input order is not part of the output contract.

items.prompt: Why is sorting often useful before duplicate-controlled combination search?

options.text: It places equal values next to each other so same-depth duplicate checks are local.
It automatically deletes duplicate occurrences.
It makes the full backtracking search linear.
It makes branch-state restoration unnecessary.

feedback.reason: Adjacent equal values allow a deterministic previous-value or i > start skip rule.

blocks.text: Sorting makes equivalence locally observable

After sorting, all occurrences of a value form one contiguous run. A loop can therefore recognize a later equal sibling by comparing candidates[i] with candidates[i - 1] instead of maintaining a depth-local set.

Sorting preserves every occurrence and does not reduce the exponential or factorial search class by itself. It is valid only when reordering candidates does not violate an original-position or order-sensitive output contract, and it does not change the need to undo shared branch state.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Sorting preserves multiplicity. The search can remain exponential. Sorting does not change mutable path semantics.

blocks.title: Normalization rule
blocks.text: Sort only when the result contract permits reordering; then adjacent equality supports a local canonical-choice rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.removes_duplicates: Sorting reorders occurrences but does not delete them; multiplicities in the input remain unchanged.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.guarantees_linear_time: Local duplicate checks may shrink the tree, but the number of distinct valid outputs can still be exponential or factorial.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.eliminates_undo: Candidate order does not change shared path mutation; append, mark, and other branch updates still require restoration.

items.prompt: In unique permutations of [1, 1, 2], why may the second 1 be chosen after the first 1 is already used in the current path?

options.text: It represents the second distinct input occurrence at a deeper position.
Duplicate control is disabled after the first choice.
The two values become unequal once one is used.
Used positions are always available again.

feedback.reason: Value-equivalent sibling starts are suppressed, but legal multiplicity inside one permutation remains.

blocks.text: The second copy is a deeper resource, not a sibling substitute
At the root of [1a, 1b, 2], starting with 1b while 1a is unused duplicates the branch starting with 1a, so 1b is skipped there.

After 1a is chosen, used[1a] is true. At the next depth, choosing unused 1b consumes the second occurrence and can build [1, 1, 2]. The values remain equal and the rule remains active; its previous-equal-used condition now permits legal multiplicity.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Duplicate control remains active but is depth-sensitive. Their values remain equal. Used positions cannot be selected twice.

blocks.title: Depth rule
blocks.text: An equal later index is skipped as a sibling representative, not when it supplies a distinct deeper occurrence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_rule_disabled: The rule remains active at every depth; its used-state condition distinguishes sibling equivalence from deeper multiplicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_become_different: Using one occurrence changes its availability, not its value; both inputs still carry value 1.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.used_means_available: A used index cannot be selected again. The legal choice is the separate unused index of the second occurrence.

items.prompt: A combinations solver skips a candidate whenever its value already appears anywhere in the current path. What valid result can this wrongly remove?

options.text: A combination containing two separate allowed occurrences of the same value.
Only combinations with all distinct values.
The empty combination.
Every sorted combination.

feedback.reason: Path-level value uniqueness is stronger than same-depth output deduplication.

blocks.text: A path-wide value ban changes the result contract
If the input contains two indexed copies of value 1 and combinations may consume both, [1, 1] is a valid result. Each occurrence is used once, so no resource-reuse rule is broken.

Rejecting a candidate merely because value 1 already appears in the path forbids the second copy and removes [1, 1]. Same-depth skipping instead removes alternate constructions of the same combination while allowing the second occurrence in a child.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Those do not contain a repeated path value. No candidate skip is evaluated for an already complete empty path. Sorting and multiplicity are separate.

blocks.title: Contract rule
blocks.text: Do not infer value uniqueness from output deduplication; preserve every multiplicity the input and result contract allow.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_distinct_only: Those do not contain a repeated path value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.empty_combination: No candidate skip is evaluated for an already complete empty path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_result: Sorting determines canonical order but does not imply that repeated values are forbidden, so it is not the class selectively removed by this bug.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly separates duplicate control from visited-state control?

options.text: Duplicate control suppresses equivalent outputs; visited state prevents illegal reuse within one path.
They are always the same condition.
Visited state exists only to deduplicate completed results.
Duplicate control exists only for graph cycles.

feedback.reason: One mechanism preserves result uniqueness, while the other preserves path legality.

blocks.text: Uniqueness of outputs and legality of paths are separate
Visited or used state answers whether this exact index, node, or cell may be used again on the active path. It prevents illegal resource reuse even when every value is distinct.

Duplicate control answers whether two different legal index branches encode the same value-level output. A unique-permutation solver uses both: used[i] enforces one use per index, while the sorted equal-sibling rule selects a canonical representative among interchangeable occurrences.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: They address different semantic problems. Visited state usually enforces branch legality. It commonly appears in combinations and permutations.

blocks.title: Diagnostic question
blocks.text: Ask whether the defect repeats a resource within one path or repeats an equivalent completed value sequence; the required rule differs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_rule: Used-state checks index reuse on the active path, while duplicate control compares legal branches for value-equivalent outputs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_only_outputs: Visited state normally protects path legality before completion, such as preventing one index or cell from being reused.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates_only_cycles: Duplicate outputs also arise in combinations and permutations of repeated values, even when no graph or cycle exists.

items.prompt: Which techniques can prevent duplicate combination results? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sort candidates and skip equal sibling choices at the same recursion depth.
Advance the start index so the same index set is not generated in different orders.
Allow equal values at different depths only when distinct occurrences and the contract permit them.
Reject every candidate whose value appears anywhere in the path.

feedback.reason: Unique combination generation requires both order canonicalization and depth-scoped value handling.

blocks.text: Unique combinations need canonical order and canonical value siblings

items: A monotonic start boundary gives each index set one increasing construction order.
Sorting plus same-depth equal skipping gives each value choice one representative sibling.
Contract-aware multiplicity permits a later equal occurrence at a deeper depth when the result may contain it.

blocks.text: These mechanisms solve different duplication sources: reordered indices, equal-valued sibling starts, and accidental over-skipping. A path-wide no-equal-values rule is too strong whenever two distinct occurrences may legally appear together.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: This can remove valid repeated-value combinations.

blocks.title: Canonicalization layers
blocks.text: Canonicalize index order and same-depth value choice without deleting legal input multiplicity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_equal_any_depth: A distinct equal occurrence may be legal at a deeper result position, so a path-wide ban removes valid repeated-value combinations.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sort_same_depth_skip: This chooses one representative branch per value at that depth.

items.prompt: Which conditions belong to the standard sorted unique-permutation skip rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: The candidate has a previous input position.
The candidate value equals the previous sorted value.
The previous equal position is not used in the current path.
The current index itself is unused.

feedback.reason: Unique-permutation legality combines ordinary unused-index state with a duplicate sibling condition.

blocks.text: The complete unique-permutation candidate test

items: current_unused is ordinary path legality: the same index cannot appear twice.
i > 0 establishes that a previous sorted position exists before it is read.
previous_not_used means the earlier equal occurrence was also available at this depth and already represents this sibling value.

blocks.text: Operationally, skip when used[i] is true; otherwise skip the duplicate sibling when i > 0, values[i] = values[i - 1], and used[i - 1] is false. If used[i - 1] is true, the later equal occurrence may legally fill a deeper position.

blocks.title: Check every required condition
blocks.text: Dropping current_unused permits index reuse. Dropping the equal-sibling condition emits duplicates. Reversing previous_not_used over-skips the legitimate second occurrence after the first is already in the path.

blocks.title: Implementation rule
blocks.text: First enforce unused-index legality, then suppress a later equal sibling only when its earlier equal representative is unused.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.i_greater_zero: A previous equal value must exist before it can define an equivalent sibling.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.equal_previous: Only equal values create value-equivalent starts.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.previous_not_used: That means the earlier equal value was available to start the equivalent sibling branch.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.current_unused: Every permutation candidate must be unused.

items.prompt: Which test inputs are useful for duplicate-control review? Select all that apply.

options.text: All values are distinct.
All values are equal.
Some values repeat while others are unique.
Only a single trivial input and no other cases.

feedback.reason: Review should cover no duplicates, maximal duplicates, and mixed multiplicity.

blocks.text: Test both under-skipping and over-skipping

items: All distinct values verify that duplicate logic does not remove ordinary legal branches.
All equal values maximize equivalent index paths while still requiring the allowed multiplicity in each full result.
Mixed counts verify selective skipping: repeated groups are canonicalized while unique values remain unaffected.

blocks.text: Compare the emitted results with the contract's expected value-distinct set and check that each appears once. A single one-value input exercises neither mixed sibling groups nor the deeper-use boundary and cannot validate the rule.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A trivial singleton cannot reveal whether the implementation suppresses equivalent siblings, preserves a second equal occurrence at depth, or leaves unique values unaffected.

blocks.title: Minimum test matrix
blocks.text: Cover zero duplicate groups, one maximal group, and mixed group sizes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_one_value: A single trivial input has no competing equal siblings or mixed multiplicity, so it cannot expose depth-scoping defects.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_distinct: It verifies that duplicate logic does not remove ordinary branches.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_equal: It stresses maximal branch equivalence and multiplicity.

items.prompt: Which statements distinguish proactive duplicate prevention from result-set deduplication? Select all that apply.

options.text: Proactive prevention can avoid exploring equivalent branches.
Result-set deduplication removes repeated outputs only after they are generated.
A result set may require hashing and storing completed outputs.
Both methods necessarily visit the same number of search states.

feedback.reason: The approaches may produce the same final value set but have different search and memory costs.

blocks.text: Same output set, different work profile

items: Proactive prevention recognizes equivalence before recursion and can remove an entire duplicate subtree.
Result-set deduplication first generates and copies the repeated output, then discovers that its key already exists.
The set retains or hashes completed length-n values, adding comparison and storage cost.

blocks.text: Both strategies can produce the same final value-distinct set, but only a proven proactive rule reduces the search tree itself. Their visited-state counts are therefore not necessarily equal.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: If k indexed branches encode one value-level subtree, proactive prevention explores one representative, whereas post-hoc deduplication may traverse all k before collapsing their outputs.

blocks.title: Cost rule
blocks.text: Where equivalence is provable at a parent, prevent the redundant subtree before paying for it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_performance: Proactive control may remove equivalent subtrees at their root, while post-hoc deduplication still visits and copies their descendants.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.prevention_smaller_tree: The search tree itself becomes smaller.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.result_set_after_work: Equivalent search work has already occurred.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.set_memory: Deduplication has additional memory and comparison cost.

items.prompt: Arrange the duplicate-controlled combination candidate flow for sorted input.

elements.text: Iterate candidate indices from the current start boundary.
If i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1], skip this sibling.
Choose the candidate and recurse with start = i + 1.
Undo the choice and continue to the next index.

feedback.reason: The duplicate check is evaluated in the parent loop before creating an equivalent sibling branch.

blocks.text: Check equality before creating the sibling branch

items: Iterate i from the current start boundary, defining the sibling candidates for one parent prefix.
If i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1], skip this later equal sibling.
Otherwise append candidates[i] and recurse with start = i + 1 so indices increase.
Pop the choice after recursion, then continue the parent loop with its prefix restored.

blocks.text: The equality check occurs before mutation because the rejected branch should never exist. Passing i + 1 and later popping serve separate invariants: canonical index order and sibling state isolation.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Iterate candidate indices from the current start boundary. Then If i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1], skip this sibling. Then Choose the candidate and recurse with start = i + 1. Then Undo the choice and continue to the next index. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Flow invariant
blocks.text: Reject equivalent siblings before choose; restore accepted branches before the next iteration.

items.prompt: A multiset contains n values with multiplicities c1, c2, ..., cm. Select the number of distinct full permutations and maximum recursion depth.
constraints: Each multiplicity ci is a positive integer and c1 + c2 + ... + cm = n.
All occurrences are used exactly once.
Outputs differing only by swapping equal values are considered identical.

feedback.reason: Equal-value swaps do not create new value sequences, reducing n! indexed permutations by multiplicity factorials.

blocks.text: Divide indexed permutations by equal-value symmetries

If all n occurrences were distinct, there would be n! index permutations. For a value occurring c1 times, permuting those c1 indistinguishable occurrences among their occupied positions produces c1! index orders with the same value sequence.
The same symmetry applies independently to every multiplicity group, so each value-distinct sequence is counted c1!c2!...cm! times among indexed permutations. Dividing gives n!/(c1!c2!...cm!).
Every complete output still fills n positions one per recursive level, so maximum recursion depth is O(n). The smaller number of leaves does not shorten an individual full permutation.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: 2^n counts subset membership decisions, and n^n allows unrestricted reuse. Neither models using all multiset occurrences exactly once.

blocks.title: Multiset formula
blocks.text: Start with n! labeled arrangements and divide by the factorial of each indistinguishable multiplicity.

items.prompt: An implementation generates all n! indexed permutations, copies each length-n path, and deduplicates them afterward, even though only u value-distinct permutations exist. Select an upper bound on generation-and-copy work and final output space.
constraints: Every indexed permutation is generated before deduplication.
Each generated path copy has length n.

feedback.reason: Post-hoc deduplication does not avoid generating and copying duplicate indexed paths.

blocks.text: Separate generation cost from retained unique output
The implementation deliberately visits all n! indexed leaves. At each leaf it copies n values and hashes or compares a length-n key, so generation-and-copy work is O(n · n!).

After deduplication, only u value-distinct paths remain, each with n stored values. The final output payload therefore uses O(un) space, excluding transient recursion state and hash-table overhead of lower order relative to stored keys.
The two dimensions use different counts: n! paths are processed before equality is known, but only u outputs survive. O(un) generation work incorrectly assumes duplicates were prevented proactively.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(n!) omits the O(n) copy or key-processing cost per leaf. O(n · n!) final space counts discarded duplicates rather than the stated retained output.

blocks.title: Accounting rule
blocks.text: Charge work to every generated indexed path; charge final output space only to the u retained value-distinct paths.
